title: HE TRUSTED GOD WHEN AN ARMY CAME AGAINST HIM… BUT WHEN SICKNESS ENTERED HIS BODY, HE LOOKED EVERYWHERE EXCEPT TO GOD.
paragraphs: HE TRUSTED GOD WHEN AN ARMY CAME AGAINST HIM… BUT WHEN SICKNESS ENTERED HIS BODY, HE LOOKED EVERYWHERE EXCEPT TO GOD.

The heartbreaking story of King Asa reveals how a man can experience extraordinary victories through faith, yet slowly lose the very dependence on God that once made him strong. And the most frightening part? His story may be closer to ours than we want to admit.
There is something deeply unsettling about the final chapter of King Asa’s life.
Not because he became sick.
Not because he sought medical treatment.
But because the man who once cried out to God when an overwhelming army threatened to destroy him eventually reached a place where Scripture could say something devastating about his heart.
“Yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.” — 2 Chronicles 16:12 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Slowly.
Because they were not written about a pagan king who had never known God.
They were written about a man who had experienced God's deliverance.
A man who had witnessed what prayer could accomplish when human strength was not enough.
A man who had once led a nation back toward the Lord.
And somehow, somewhere along the road, something changed.
The king who once knew where to run when he was helpless had begun relying on everything except the One who had rescued him.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question in this entire story is not, “Why did Asa seek physicians?”
Perhaps it is this:
How does someone who has seen God move so powerfully eventually learn to live as though he no longer needs Him?
Because that question is not only about an ancient king.
It is about the Christian who once prayed before making every major decision but now trusts personal judgment without seeking God's wisdom.
It is about the believer who once opened Scripture with trembling hands but now goes days without listening to what God has said.
It is about the person who once wept in worship but has become so occupied with surviving life that intimacy with God has quietly been pushed aside.
And maybe, if we are willing to be painfully honest, it is about us.
King Asa did not begin his reign as a man indifferent to God.
Quite the opposite.

Second Chronicles 14 tells us that Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the Lord. He removed foreign altars, broke down objects associated with idolatrous worship, and commanded Judah to seek the Lord and obey His commandments.
He was not merely talking about faith.
He was taking action.
He understood that spiritual compromise was dangerous and that a nation could not expect the blessing of covenant faithfulness while deliberately embracing the worship of false gods.
Then came a moment that would expose whether Asa truly believed the God he was calling his people to worship.
A massive enemy force approached Judah.

According to 2 Chronicles 14:9, Zerah the Ethiopian came against Asa with an army described in the Hebrew text as eleph alaphim (אֶלֶף אֲלָפִים), literally “a thousand thousands,” traditionally understood as a million men.
The precise historical scale of the force is debated, but the biblical narrative is unmistakable: Asa faced a terrifying military threat.
This was not a situation he could confidently control.
His army was outmatched.
His resources were limited.
His future was uncertain.
And this is where we meet the Asa who makes his later downfall so heartbreaking.
He prayed.
Not a polished prayer designed to impress people.
Not a religious performance.
A desperate declaration of dependence.
“LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee.” — 2 Chronicles 14:11 (KJV)
For we rest on thee.
Those words carry the heartbeat of his early faith.
In the Hebrew text, Asa says:
כִּי־עָלֶיךָ נִשְׁעַנּוּ
Ki ‘alekha nish‘annu.
“For we lean upon You,” or “For we rely upon You.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root שׁען (sha‘an), conveying the idea of leaning upon or depending on someone for support.
Imagine a wounded soldier who cannot stand without another person's strength.
Imagine someone exhausted beyond words, finally allowing themselves to be supported.
That is the picture.
Asa understood something many believers only remember when life falls apart.
Faith is not pretending we are strong. Faith is knowing upon whom we must lean when we are not.
And the Lord delivered Judah.
Second Chronicles 14:12 records that the Lord struck the enemy before Asa and Judah.
The victory belonged to God.
Asa had discovered that his greatest security was not the number of soldiers standing behind him but the Lord upon whom he depended.
Yet the story did not end there.
In 2 Chronicles 15, the prophet Azariah delivered a message that should have remained engraved upon Asa's heart.
“The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.” — 2 Chronicles 15:2 (KJV)

These words were spoken within the covenant setting of Judah's relationship with God. They were a serious call to faithfulness, not a formula suggesting that every suffering believer has been abandoned by the Lord.
Asa responded with renewed courage.
He removed detestable idols, repaired the altar of the Lord, and gathered the people into a renewed commitment to seek God.
The nation rejoiced.
Scripture tells us that they sought the Lord with their whole desire, and He was found by them.
There was peace.
There was restoration.
There was renewed worship.
If the account had ended there, Asa's life would have been remembered as an almost uncomplicated example of spiritual courage.
But Scripture is honest about its heroes.
It does not hide their failures to protect their reputations.
It tells the truth because we need the truth.
And what happened next should make every Christian examine the condition of their heart.
Years later, Baasha, king of Israel, began fortifying Ramah, threatening Judah's access and movement.
Asa faced another national crisis.

But this time, instead of recording a prayer like the one he had offered against Zerah, Scripture tells us that he took silver and gold from the treasures of the Lord's house and the royal palace and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria.
He wanted Ben-hadad to break his alliance with Baasha.
The strategy worked in the immediate military sense.
Ben-hadad attacked cities of Israel.
Baasha abandoned his building project.
Asa dismantled the fortifications at Ramah and used the materials elsewhere.
From a purely political perspective, it looked like a successful maneuver.
The threat had been neutralized.
The plan had produced results.
But God saw something the outward victory concealed.
The prophet Hanani came to Asa with a rebuke.
“Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.” — 2 Chronicles 16:7 (KJV)
Notice that word.
Relied.
The same essential idea that had once described Asa's dependence upon God now exposed his dependence upon a foreign king.
Earlier, he had leaned upon the Lord.
Now he was leaning upon political power.
And this is where the story begins to reach into places we would rather keep hidden.
Because not every form of spiritual decline looks like open rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like competence without prayer.
Sometimes it looks like success without surrender.
Sometimes it looks like a person who still believes in God but has stopped depending upon Him.
We can become so experienced at solving problems that we forget to seek the One who gave us wisdom in the first place.
We can become so familiar with church that we stop being amazed by Christ.
We can become so busy doing things for God that we neglect communion with God.
And because life may continue functioning, we assume nothing is wrong.
The bills are being paid.
The responsibilities are being handled.
The ministry is moving.
The family is surviving.
Everything looks fine.
Except that somewhere inside, the heart is no longer leaning where it once leaned.
And the tragedy is that spiritual independence can feel like maturity when it is actually becoming distance.
Hanani reminded Asa of his earlier victory.
Had the Lord not delivered the overwhelming army into his hand?
Then came one of the most beautiful declarations in the entire Old Testament.
“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.” — 2 Chronicles 16:9 (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated “perfect” is שָׁלֵם (shalem).
In this context, it carries the sense of being whole, complete, or fully devoted.
It does not mean that God is searching only for people who have never made mistakes.
It speaks of hearts undivided in their loyalty to Him.
God was not asking Asa to become self-sufficient.
He was calling him back to wholehearted dependence.
And here is the astonishing truth.
The God who had delivered Asa before had not become weaker.
The Lord had not lost His power.
His faithfulness had not diminished.
The change was in Asa.
The king who once rested in God had begun trusting his own arrangements.
And when the prophet confronted him, Asa did something even more disturbing.
He became angry.
He imprisoned Hanani.
He oppressed some of the people.
Think about that.
The man who once humbled himself before God now resisted the messenger who called him to repentance.
And that is one of the most dangerous moments in a believer's life.
Not when someone exposes a sin.
But when our pride becomes more precious to us than the truth that could bring us back.
Sometimes the warning we resent is the very mercy we desperately need.
A sermon makes us uncomfortable, so we dismiss the preacher.
A Scripture exposes our compromise, so we avoid reading it.
A trusted friend confronts us, so we accuse them of judging.
Our conscience troubles us, so we fill our lives with more noise.
We would rather silence the warning than surrender the behavior.
And all the while, the Lord is calling us to return.
Then comes the verse that gives this story its haunting conclusion.

“And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.” — 2 Chronicles 16:12 (KJV)
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa developed a serious disease in his feet.
The Hebrew text describes the illness as severe, but it does not identify a precise medical diagnosis.
We should not invent one.
Some have speculated about gout, infection, or other conditions, but Scripture does not tell us.
What Scripture does tell us is far more important than the name of the disease.
It tells us where Asa did not turn.
The Hebrew phrase is:
וְגַם־בְּחָלְיוֹ לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה כִּי בָּרֹפְאִים
Ve-gam be-cholyo lo-darash et-YHWH ki ba-rof'im.
“Yet even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians.”
The verb דָּרַשׁ (darash) means to seek, inquire of, or consult.
It is a significant word in Chronicles, where seeking the Lord is repeatedly associated with covenant faithfulness and dependence upon Him.
And the word רֹפְאִים (rof'im) means physicians or healers.
But we must be extremely careful here.
The sin of Asa was not simply that he went to physicians. The passage condemns his failure to seek the Lord.
That distinction matters.
It matters for the Christian sitting in a hospital waiting room.
It matters for the mother praying beside a sick child.
It matters for the believer taking prescribed medication.
It matters for the person undergoing chemotherapy, dialysis, surgery, rehabilitation, or long-term treatment.
Please hear this clearly.
Seeking medical care is not a betrayal of faith.
Scripture does not command believers to reject physicians.
Jesus Himself said, “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick” (Luke 5:31, KJV). He was using the familiar role of physicians to explain His mission to sinners.
Luke, a companion of Paul, is called “the beloved physician” in Colossians 4:14.
And Paul instructed Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23), showing that practical remedies were not inherently opposed to faith.
The biblical issue is not medicine versus prayer.
It is whether we acknowledge and trust God while making use of the ordinary means available to us.
We can pray before surgery and thank God for the surgeon.
We can trust the Lord while taking medicine.
We can seek divine wisdom and qualified medical advice without treating them as enemies.
And we must never assume that someone remains sick because they did not pray hard enough.
The apostle Paul himself pleaded with the Lord concerning his thorn in the flesh, and God's answer was not the removal of that affliction but the promise:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
Faith does not guarantee that every illness disappears.
And physical healing is not the measure of God's love.
The Lord is sovereign in both healing and suffering.
So what made Asa's conduct so tragic?
The context.
His earlier reliance upon a foreign king.
His rejection of prophetic correction.
His anger.
His imprisonment of God's messenger.
And now, even in severe illness, the chronicler records that he did not seek the Lord.
This was not presented as an isolated medical decision.
It was the final expression of a pattern of misplaced dependence.
Asa had become a man who could seek assistance while neglecting the God he once trusted.
And that is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because there are people reading these words who have been asking everyone for advice except the Lord.
You have talked to friends.
You have searched for answers.
You have consulted professionals.
You have watched videos, read articles, and exhausted yourself trying to find a way forward.
Some of those steps may be wise and necessary.
But somewhere along the way, prayer became an afterthought.
You have spent hours worrying about what could happen and barely a moment bringing your fears before your heavenly Father.
You have become familiar with your problems and distant from His promises.
And maybe you have not stopped believing in Jesus.
You have simply stopped bringing your whole life to Him.
That is a frightening place to be.
Because we can still speak Christian language while living in practical independence from Christ.
We can still say “God is good” while refusing to trust Him with what hurts.
We can still share Bible verses while privately resisting the very Word we publish.
We can still worship publicly while protecting hidden areas of disobedience.
And God sees what nobody else sees.
Not merely to expose us.
But to call us back.
Perhaps your greatest crisis today is not the situation you are desperately trying to escape.
Perhaps it is that the situation has revealed how far your heart has wandered from dependence upon the Lord.
But there is something else we must understand.
King Asa's story is not included in Scripture so that we can look down upon him.
It is there to warn us.
First Corinthians 10:12 says:
“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
Past victories are not a guarantee of present faithfulness.
Yesterday's obedience cannot replace today's surrender.
A testimony of what God did ten years ago does not excuse our refusal to seek Him now.
We need grace today.
We need the Word today.
We need prayer today.
We need Jesus today.
And there is a reason this story should not end with Asa's failure.
Because if it ended there, it would leave us with a warning but not the fullness of the hope revealed in the Gospel.
Asa was a king who began well and later stumbled grievously.
But Scripture points us toward another King.
A greater King.
One whose obedience did not collapse under pressure.
One who did not turn away from the Father when suffering approached.
His name is Jesus Christ.
When Jesus entered Gethsemane, He knew the suffering that awaited Him.
The cross was before Him.
Betrayal was near.
His disciples would scatter.
He would bear the judgment due to sinners.
And in the agony of that hour, Jesus prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39 (KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Asa faced suffering, and the account says he did not seek the Lord.
Jesus faced suffering beyond anything we can fully comprehend, and He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
Asa resisted the prophetic word when it exposed his failure.
Jesus fulfilled the Scriptures in perfect obedience.
Asa's final years revealed the weakness of a fallen king.
Jesus, the sinless King, remained faithful all the way to the cross.
And He did not die because He had failed.
He died for those who have.
For the proud.
For the wandering.
For the prayerless.
For those who have trusted money more than God.
For those who have trusted human approval more than truth.
For those who have relied on their own strength until their souls became exhausted.
For those who have heard the call to repent and kept delaying.
For people like us.
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Jesus bore our sins, not because He was sinful, but because He willingly became our substitute.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is why our hope does not rest upon our ability to maintain a flawless spiritual record.
Our hope rests upon the crucified and risen Christ.
And His grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is the very grace that calls us out of rebellion and transforms us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to deny ungodliness and live soberly, righteously, and godly.
Grace does not tell the wandering heart, “Stay where you are.”
Grace calls it home.
Maybe you have spent years trying to appear spiritually strong.
Maybe people know you as the one who encourages everyone else.
The one who always has a Scripture.
The one who never seems to struggle.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know the truth.
Your prayer life has become dry.
Your Bible remains closed more often than you want to admit.
You are tired.
You are carrying guilt you have never confessed.
You are struggling with a temptation you thought you had overcome.
You are trying to keep everything together, and somewhere beneath the pressure, you have begun to wonder whether God still wants to hear from you.
Listen carefully.
The Lord does not ask you to clean yourself up before coming to Christ. He calls you to come to Christ in repentance and faith, because only His grace can truly make you new.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not grounded in our worthiness.
It is grounded in God's faithfulness and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to pretend you are fine.
You do not have to hide your spiritual exhaustion.
You do not have to make another promise that you will somehow fix yourself by tomorrow.
Come honestly.
Confess what you have been defending.
Surrender what you have been protecting.
Turn away from the sin that has been pulling you from the Lord.
And trust the Savior who died and rose again to redeem sinners.
Perhaps you need to pray something as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have been leaning on everything except You. I have trusted my own understanding, protected my pride, and allowed my heart to become distant. Forgive me. Expose what I need to surrender. Teach me to seek You again, not merely when life falls apart, but in every season. Thank You for the cross, for Your mercy, and for the hope of new life through Your resurrection. Make my heart wholly Yours. Amen.”
And if this prayer describes what is happening inside you, do not rush past it.
Sit with it.
Bring your heart before the Lord.
Open His Word.
Speak with a mature believer who can encourage you in truth.
If you have been avoiding medical care because you thought trusting God meant refusing treatment, please do not carry that burden. Seek appropriate care, and seek the Lord through it all.
If you have been hiding a spiritual struggle because you fear what people will think, remember that confession and repentance are not signs that grace has failed.
They are often where the transforming work of grace becomes visible.
We are not told that Asa repented before his death.
Second Chronicles 16:13 records that he died in the forty-first year of his reign.
We must not invent a final conversation between Asa and God that Scripture does not record.
The biblical account leaves us with a sobering warning.
But while we are still alive, that warning invites a response.
Do not wait until your heart becomes so hardened that correction only makes you angry.
Do not wait until you have lost years of fellowship with God before recognizing what you have neglected.
Do not confuse religious activity with intimacy with Christ.
And do not allow the memory of yesterday's faith to replace the obedience God calls you to today.
The question is not merely whether you once trusted God. The question is whether you are seeking Him now.
Maybe that is why you needed to encounter Asa's story today.
Not to be crushed by condemnation.
But to be awakened to the mercy of God.
The same Lord who calls sinners to repentance is rich in mercy toward all who call upon Him.
And the risen Jesus still receives those who come to Him in faith.
John 6:37 records His promise:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What a Savior.
He knows the truth about us.
The pride.
The fear.
The failures.
The compromises.
The things we never tell anyone.
And yet He calls us to Himself.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because His grace makes genuine repentance possible.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
From hidden compromise to honest confession.
From self-reliance to surrender.
From spiritual exhaustion to renewed dependence upon Christ.
Not because we have the power to rewrite our own story.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior who redeems sinners and transforms lives.
And if this message has reached something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you to do more than simply read it and move on.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to reveal private details.
Sometimes a few honest words can open the door for another believer to remind you of the promises of Christ.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that restoration through Jesus Christ is possible.
Before you leave, think about one person who needs this message.
Perhaps it is a friend who has slowly drifted away from prayer.
A family member whose faith is being tested by illness.
A Christian who looks strong in public but is privately overwhelmed.
Or someone who does not yet know the hope of the Gospel.
There is also a deeper invitation I want to make, especially to those who believe that biblical discipleship should continue beyond a single article.
Gospel Warrior is working to provide Scripture-centered encouragement and discipleship resources to people who need to hear the truth about Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Word, strengthen their faith, encourage their families, and continue growing in grace.
And this work requires ongoing time, resources, and support.
It is a voluntary way to support the continuation and expansion of this ministry's work.

It helps sustain the effort to create and share biblical teaching, provide discipleship resources, and reach more people with the message of repentance, forgiveness, and salvation through Jesus Christ.

For those who choose to view this giving as part of their personal Christian stewardship, it can be an expression of generosity and an offering of support to Gospel-centered work. Scripture teaches believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But if you are able and willing, supporting sound biblical teaching and Gospel outreach can be one meaningful way of serving others for Christ's sake.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The purpose is not simply to place another Christian item on a shelf, but to help put reminders of biblical truth into homes, conversations, and everyday life.
Pray that the Lord will use His Word to awaken hearts, strengthen weary believers, and point those who are far from Him toward the Savior.
Because no ministry can save a soul.
No Christian product can transform a heart.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
And that brings us back to the king whose life began with such extraordinary dependence upon God.
Asa once stood before an overwhelming army and declared, “For we rest on thee.”
Years later, in severe illness, Scripture records that he did not seek the Lord.
What a sobering contrast.
One life.
One king.
Two very different expressions of dependence.
And now his story stands before us like a mirror.
Where are you leaning today?
On your achievements?
On your savings?
On your reputation?
On your experience?
On the approval of people?
On the belief that because you once walked closely with God, you can afford to neglect Him now?
Or are you leaning upon the Lord?
The One who never changes.
The One who sees the heart.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who gave His only begotten Son so that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.
Perhaps the most important decision you make today will not be a financial decision, a medical decision, or a professional decision.
Perhaps it will be the quiet decision to stop resisting the voice of God in Scripture.
To open your Bible again.
To confess the sin you have excused.
To seek help where you need it.
To forgive someone you have been refusing to forgive.
To surrender the control you have been desperately trying to keep.
To trust Jesus Christ not merely with the eternal destiny of your soul but with the daily obedience of your life.
And when you find yourself weak tomorrow, seek Him again.
When fear returns, seek Him again.
When the diagnosis is uncertain, seek Him again.
When the answer to prayer is delayed, seek Him again.
When success tempts you to become proud, seek Him again.
When correction hurts your ego, humble yourself and seek Him again.
Not because seeking God guarantees an easy life.
But because knowing Christ is infinitely more precious than the illusion of controlling everything.
The tragedy of Asa was not that he needed help.
We all need help.
The tragedy was that the man who once knew where to lean stopped seeking the Lord.
Do not let that become the story of your heart.
And remember this:
The most heartbreaking thing is not reaching the end of your strength. It is forgetting the Savior who invites you to depend on His.
